items.question: Does the sample look like the mix of people in whom this test would really be used, rather than obvious cases set against healthy volunteers?
items.why: Any test separates clear extremes better than it separates the ambiguous middle, so studying advanced cases against healthy controls flatters both sensitivity and specificity.

items.question: Can you tell what was used as the comparison standard, and is it strong enough to count as the truth for this condition?
items.why: Every mistake in the comparison standard is charged to the test under study, so a weak standard can make an accurate test look wrong, or a poor test look better than it is.

items.question: Do you know whether whoever read the new test could see the comparison standard result, and whether the reverse was also prevented?
items.why: Interpreters who have seen the other result drift toward agreement, which manufactures accuracy that would never appear in day-to-day practice.

items.question: Can you see that every participant was checked against the same comparison standard, including those whose test came back negative?
items.why: When only positive results are confirmed, false negatives are never counted, and sensitivity ends up calculated from a group trimmed of the test's own misses.

items.question: Does the abstract indicate that the cut-off separating a positive from a negative result was fixed in advance rather than chosen after the data were seen?
items.why: A threshold tuned on the same sample it is reported from performs worse in the next group of patients, sometimes considerably worse.

items.question: Can you tell how many results were indeterminate, failed or missing, and how they were handled in the analysis?
items.why: Quietly dropping uninterpretable results removes the hardest patients from the denominator, so a test that often fails in practice looks dependable on paper.

items.question: Are sensitivity and specificity reported with confidence intervals, and can you recover the raw counts behind them?
items.why: Accuracy estimated from a few dozen patients can move by tens of percentage points, and a single figure with no interval hides how unstable it is.

items.question: Does the report make clear how common the condition was in the sample, since that governs what a positive result actually means?
items.why: Sensitivity and specificity stay roughly steady while predictive values move with prevalence, so a test that shines in a high-prevalence sample can return mostly false positives where the condition is rare.
